subject: literacy
title: Put it all together with a new fable

activities.title: Story map, traits and message: The Fox and the Crow
materials: The Fox and the Crow (book, online text, or retell)
parentPrompts: Have your child read the fable aloud, or listen to you read it. Outline: a crow sits in a tree holding a piece of cheese; a fox wants it and flatters the crow's looks and says it must have a lovely voice; the crow opens its beak to sing and drops the cheese; the fox grabs it and runs off. Fables by Aesop are in the public domain: you can read one from a library book or a free online collection, or simply tell it in your own words using the outline here.
Without help at first, have your child draw a story map (characters, setting, problem, ending) and write a trait word for each animal with proof from the story.
Ask: "What is the central message, and which two details support it?" A possible message: be careful of people who flatter you to get something.
Offer help only where they are stuck by asking questions, not giving answers.
You will know they got it when the story map, traits, and message are complete and each uses details from the text.

activities.title: Which two fables teach the same lesson?
materials: fables read this month (reread short ones)
parentPrompts: Lay out titles of fables you have read: Tortoise and Hare, Ant and Grasshopper, Crow and Pitcher, Goose and Golden Eggs, Dog and His Reflection, Fox and Crow, North Wind and Sun. Write each on a card or scrap of paper.
Have your child sort the titles into groups that share a similar message, and write a message sentence for each group.
Ask: "Which fable fits in more than one group? Which has a message that stands alone?" Encourage friendly debate; any grouping is fine if explained with details.
Pick one group and have your child tell how the characters, settings and events differ even though the lesson is similar.
You will know they got it when they justify each group by naming the message and a supporting detail.

activities.title: Reader's theater: The Boy Who Cried Wolf
materials: a short script you and your child write (see steps)
parentPrompts: Turn The Boy Who Cried Wolf into a short play together. Make a list of speaking parts: Narrator, Boy, two Villagers. Write a few lines each on paper (for example, Boy: Wolf! Wolf! Help!).

Practice reading the lines aloud. Model reading with expression: a shout for the boy, a worried voice for the villagers, a slow and sad voice at the end. Ask them to try it again with the right feeling.
Talk about how punctuation helps: an exclamation mark means strong feeling, a question mark means your voice goes up, commas mean a small pause.
Perform it for another person. Swap parts and read it again.
You will know they got it when they read smoothly at a natural pace and change their voice to show feeling.

subject: literacy
title: Create a fable of your own

activities.title: Plan and tell your own fable
parentPrompts: Explain that a fable is a short story with animal characters that teaches a lesson. Start with the message: have your child choose a lesson such as be honest, share, or keep trying.
Make a story map: two animal characters (with traits), a setting, a problem that shows the lesson, and an ending.
Have them tell the story aloud to you first with a beginning, middle and end. Then write a short draft in order, using words like first, then, and finally.
End the draft with a sentence that says the moral, like "The moral is...". Do not worry about perfect spelling today.
You will know they got it when the events lead logically to the lesson, and the lesson fits what happened to the characters.

subject: literacy
title: Share a story and its message

activities.title: Story share: characters, events and message
materials: a favorite story or fable from this unit
story map and drawings made this month
an audience (family member, friend, or toy)
parentPrompts: Have your child choose one favorite story from the unit. Help them gather their story map, notes and any drawings.

They tell the audience: the title, the characters and their traits, the main events in order, and the central message with one detail that proves it. Remind them to speak clearly at a steady pace and in complete sentences.
The audience asks one or two questions. Teach your child to answer and give a detail, for example, "The story says the grasshopper had no food when winter came."
Finish by celebrating what they have learned. Ask: "What was the hardest part of finding a message? What helped you?"
You will know they got it when they present all four parts clearly and answer questions with details.

activities.title: Choose a fable and plan an opinion about it
parentPrompts: Explain that opinion writing can be about a text. Ask your child to choose a fable and decide: "Do you think the message is a good lesson to follow? Which character do you like best? Was the ending fair?"
Have them write one opinion sentence that includes the title of the fable. Remind them that titles of stories have capital letters on the important words.
Plan two reasons, and for each one write a detail or action from the story as evidence (for example, the crow was clever because it dropped pebbles into the pitcher).
Check the plan: Does each reason come from the story? Is there a place to use because?
You will know they got it when the plan has an opinion about a story and two reasons with details from the text.

subject: literacy
title: Draft and polish the story opinion

activities.title: Write the opinion about the fable
parentPrompts: Have your child use the plan to write an introduction with the story title and opinion, two reasons with details, linking words, and a conclusion.
When done, reread the piece aloud and use the checklist from week 3 to check each part.
Fix capital letters, ending marks and spelling. They can use a dictionary for any word they are unsure of.
Copy it neatly or type it, with your help on keyboarding. Add a drawing from the story if they like.
You will know they got it when the piece states an opinion, gives story-based reasons, links them, and ends well.

activities.title: Read aloud and reflect
parentPrompts: Have your child read their writing aloud to an audience at a clear pace, looking up at the listener sometimes.
The audience says one thing they liked and asks one question. Teach your child to answer in a complete sentence.
Ask: "Did anyone change their mind or learn something? Which of your reasons is strongest?"
Reflect: have them write three sentences about what they learned about opinion writing, for example, what helped them the most and what they want to practice next.
You will know they got it when they read aloud clearly and can name the parts of an opinion piece in their own words.

activities.title: Sort words by their endings
parentPrompts: Explain that many longer words end with -tion (said "shun") and -ture (said "cher"). These endings come from Latin. -tion usually shows an action or the result of an action, and -ture often makes a noun.

Write twelve words: action, vacation, invention, collection, direction, picture, nature, adventure, creature, future, capture, mixture. Have your child read each aloud, splitting before the ending (va-ca-tion, ad-ven-ture).
Sort them into two piles by ending. Ask: "What do you notice about how the ending sounds?"
Find the base word in some words: collect/collection, invent/invention, direct/direction. Talk about how the meaning is related.
You will know they got it when they read the endings smoothly and find the base word in a new word.

activities.title: Big-word sentence challenge
materials: a short passage or book at the third-grade level
parentPrompts: Choose a page of a book with several long words. Have your child read it aloud. When they get to a long word, coach them to look for prefixes, suffixes, and syllables, and then read the whole word.
Write down five long words they found on sticky notes and have them split each into parts and use it in a new sentence.
Review words that do not follow the usual patterns, such as said, friend, laugh, thought, and again. Have your child read each one and use it in a sentence.
Play a quick game: you read a sentence with a mistake in one long word, and they correct it.
You will know they got it when they read long words by chunking them and correct their own reading when it does not make sense.

activities.title: Make equal groups with paper plates
materials: paper plates or circles drawn on paper
20 to 30 counters (buttons, dried beans, or paper squares; supervise young siblings)
parentPrompts: Put 3 counters on each of 4 plates. Say: "4 groups of 3." Explain that multiplication is a way to find the total when groups are equal: 4 x 3 means 4 groups with 3 in each group.
Count the total (12) and write 4 x 3 = 12. Then make 3 plates with 5 counters and write 3 x 5 = 15.
Make different groups and have them write the multiplication sentence. Ask: "What does the first number tell you? What does the second tell you?"
Show an unequal set (2, 3, 4) and ask: "Can we write a multiplication sentence for this? Why not?"
You will know they got it when they say each multiplication as groups of and write the matching sentence.

activities.title: Build arrays and find the total
parentPrompts: Explain: an array puts equal groups in rows and columns. Build 3 rows with 4 in each row. Ask: "How many rows? How many in each row? How many in all?" Write 3 x 4 = 12.
Turn the array on its side to get 4 rows of 3. Notice that the total is still 12 (4 x 3 = 12). Ask: "What do you notice?"
Build arrays for 2 x 6, 5 x 3, and 4 x 4 and write each sentence.
Look for arrays in the house, such as egg cartons, muffin tins, or window panes. Count the rows and columns of each.
You will know they got it when they build an array from a multiplication sentence and write a sentence from an array.

activities.title: Jumps on a number line
parentPrompts: Draw a number line from 0 to 20. Show 4 groups of 3 by making 4 jumps of 3, landing on 3, 6, 9, 12. Write the addition: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12, and the multiplication: 4 x 3 = 12.
Have them make jumps for 5 x 2, 3 x 5, and 6 x 2 (on a longer line). For each, write both sentences.
Ask: "Why is multiplication quicker than adding the same number again and again?"
Skip count aloud by 2s, 5s, and 10s to 50, and by 3s to 30.
You will know they got it when they link jumps, repeated addition, and multiplication.

activities.title: Stories for multiplication and sharing equally
parentPrompts: Read: "There are 5 bags with 4 apples in each. How many apples in all?" Act out the groups with counters and write 5 x 4 = 20.
Now try sharing: "12 stickers are shared equally among 3 friends. How many does each get?" Deal the counters one at a time into 3 groups. Write 12 / 3 = 4 and tell that this is sharing equally.
Have your child write one multiplication story and one sharing story, then solve them.
Ask: "How is sharing equally like finding groups?" (Both involve equal groups, but you are finding a different unknown.)
You will know they got it when they set up equal groups, write the sentence, and solve.

activities.title: Market day: mixed review game
materials: 5 to 10 household items with price tags from 20 to 500
parentPrompts: Set up a play market with items priced up to 500 and give your child money in hundreds, tens, and ones. Choose two items to buy: have them add the prices and pay.
Next they sell: you buy something and give a larger amount, and they work out the change by subtracting.
Include a multiplication question: "I want 4 packs of 3 pencils. How many pencils?" and a rounding question: "About how much is the total to the nearest 100?"
Switch roles and let them set prices. Ask them to explain how they found each answer.
You will know they got it when they correctly add, subtract, round, and use equal groups, and can explain their thinking.

activities.title: Design a marble-style run
parentPrompts: Challenge: build a track that makes a small ball travel at least 1 meter and stop in a target area, like a box. Safety: keep the ball larger than a mouth and watch small siblings.
Have your child sketch a plan, then build it. Test and watch where the ball goes.
If the ball does not reach the target, change one thing at a time (ramp angle, surface) and test again.
Ask: "Which forces were acting? Which change worked best? Why?"
You will know they got it when they improve their design by changing one thing at a time and can explain the forces.

activities.title: Graph the ramp results
materials: data from the ramp lessons (or collect new data)
parentPrompts: Look at the table from the ramp or pendulum test. Choose one to graph.
Make a bar graph: label the bottom with the ramp heights (or string lengths) and the side with the distances (or swings). Draw a bar for each.
Ask: "What pattern does the graph show? Which bar is the tallest?" Use the pattern to predict a new value and test it if you can.
Write two sentences: one describing the pattern and one saying what you predict next.
You will know they got it when the graph is correct and their prediction comes from the pattern.

activities.title: Teach it back
materials: a toy car and a ball
parentPrompts: Look back at your notes and charts from the unit. Ask: "What did you learn about pushes and pulls, balanced and unbalanced forces, friction, and patterns in motion?"
Have your child make a poster or a notebook page with three headings: Forces, Balanced and unbalanced, Patterns in motion. They write one fact and draw one picture under each.
They explain it to a family member and demonstrate with a toy car or a ball.
Ask: "What question would you like to investigate next?" Write it down.
You will know they got it when they use words like force, friction, balanced and pattern correctly and show an example for each.

subject: social-studies
title: Why people live where they do

activities.title: Research a community type
materials: library books, an atlas, or a trusted website
parentPrompts: Explain: a community is a group of people who live in the same place. Communities can be in a city, in the country, or somewhere in between. Land, water, and roads affect where people build.
Choose one place (your own or another) and look up three facts about it, such as nearby water, land features, or jobs. Take brief notes.
Ask: "How do the land and water around it help people? Which jobs or places are there because of it?"
Write three sentences about why people live there and read them aloud.
You will know they got it when they use facts from a source and explain how the place helps people meet their needs.

activities.title: Make a poster and present it
parentPrompts: Have your child make a poster about your community with a map, a key, a compass rose, and three labeled places.
Add a section with two facts about the land or water near you and one about the people who help the community.
They present the poster to family and explain how to read the map and where things are. Remind them to speak clearly and use complete sentences.
Ask: "What did you learn about maps? What would you like to explore on a map?"
You will know they got it when the poster has a correct map and they can read it aloud.
